overview.title: Too much capacity, and the turn to generalization
overview.main_topic: An oversized MNIST MLP (3×2,048 units) that overfits from the first epoch, and the transition to section 5.4
overview.central_idea: Overparameterization is normal in deep learning, but too much memorization capacity shows up as overfitting right away. Once a model generalizes somewhat and can overfit, the focus switches to maximizing generalization.
overview.importance: This completes the three-case capacity comparison (too little, about right, too much) and marks the boundary between the two phases of the workflow: improving fit, then improving generalization.
learning_objectives: Recognize 'overfits right away' as the sign of too much capacity.
Read the very-large-model code and estimate its parameter count (about 10 million).
Explain why the batch size was reduced to 32 for the larger model.
State when to switch from improving fit to improving generalization.

summary:
The page first adds a caveat to the "make it bigger" advice of p.181. It is *standard* to work with models that are "way overparameterized for the problem at hand," yet there can be such a thing as ***too much* memorization capacity**. The symptom is specific: **the model starts overfitting right away**.

The demonstration is an MNIST MLP with **three intermediate layers of 2,048 ReLU units each** plus a 10-way softmax output. Compile settings are unchanged (rmsprop, sparse categorical crossentropy, accuracy), and training again runs 20 epochs with `validation_split=0.2`. One thing differs: `batch_size=32`. A margin callout explains that *when training larger models, you can reduce the batch size to limit memory consumption*. The history is stored in `history_very_large_model`.

**Figure 5.16** ("Effect of excessive model capacity on validation loss") shows the validation loss at its lowest, about 0.12, after the very first epoch. It then rises jaggedly, to about 0.15-0.16 around epochs 7-12 and to about 0.20 at epochs 14 and 20. There is no initial phase of improvement, unlike Figure 5.15. The curve is also noisier.

The page then opens **section 5.4, Improving generalization**: once a model "has shown to have some generalization power and to be able to overfit," you switch your focus to *maximizing generalization*. The following subsections cover dataset curation (p.183), feature engineering (p.183), early stopping (p.185) and regularization (p.185).

Together with pp.180-181, this page gives a complete picture. Too little capacity stalls (0.26 plateau). Appropriate capacity dips then rises (minimum about 0.09). Excessive capacity overfits immediately (best about 0.12, then worse).

paragraphs.excerpt: Note that while it is standard to work with models that are way overparameterized
paragraphs.what_it_says: Overparameterized models are standard, but too much memorization capacity is possible. You can tell a model is too large when it starts overfitting right away. The example is an MNIST model with three 2,048-unit intermediate layers (Figure 5.16).
paragraphs.what_it_means: 'Bigger' has limits. A huge model memorizes the 48,000 training images so quickly that its best validation score comes after the first epoch, and every later epoch fits noise.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It gives a concrete diagnostic for the upper end of the capacity range and motivates capacity reduction as a regularizer (p.187).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: this model has about 10.0 million parameters (784·2048+2048 + 2·(2048·2048+2048) + 2048·10+10 = 10,020,874), roughly 85× the 2×128 model and over 200 parameters per training image.

terminology.meaning: Having more parameters than seemingly needed for the task, often more than there are training samples. This is common in deep learning and not automatically harmful.
The ability to store specific training examples (and their noise) rather than general rules.

connections: p.181: the 2×128 model overfits only after about eight epochs
p.188: on IMDb, a much bigger model likewise overfits after one epoch and its validation loss is noisier

paragraphs.why_it_matters: It tells you when to change strategy, from adding capacity to curating data, engineering features, stopping early and regularizing.

concepts.name: Excessive capacity
concepts.definition: More memorization capacity than the problem needs, so the model begins memorizing training-specific noise almost immediately.
concepts.intuition: A student with a photographic memory who memorizes the answer key on day one instead of learning the method.
concepts.technical: Diagnostic: the validation loss is lowest at epoch 1 or 2 and rises from there (Figure 5.16), often noisily.
concepts.significance: It completes the capacity spectrum and shows why capacity must be tuned, not only maximized.
concepts.example: 3×Dense(2048): best validation loss about 0.12 at epoch 1, about 0.20 by epoch 20.
concepts.misconception: That overparameterization is always bad. The book says it is standard; it becomes too much only when overfitting is immediate.

concepts.name: Batch size and memory
concepts.definition: The number of samples per gradient update. It sets how many activations must be held in memory at once.
concepts.intuition: Carry fewer boxes per trip when the boxes get heavier.
concepts.technical: Activation memory scales with batch_size × layer widths. With 2,048-unit layers, smaller batches keep memory in check. Smaller batches also give noisier gradients and more updates per epoch.
concepts.significance: The code callout gives practical advice: reduce batch size when training larger models.
concepts.misconception: That batch size only affects speed. It also affects memory and gradient noise (p.179: larger batches give less noisy gradients).

concepts.name: Shifting focus to generalization
concepts.definition: The second phase of the workflow, which starts once the model can overfit: maximize performance on unseen data.
concepts.intuition: First prove you can reach the boundary, then step back to the sweet spot.
concepts.technical: The tools are dataset curation, feature engineering, early stopping and regularization (sections 5.4.1-5.4.4).
concepts.significance: It defines the structure of the rest of chapter 5.
concepts.example: Moving from Figure 5.15's U-curve to stopping at its minimum or adding regularization.
concepts.misconception: That you should regularize from the very start. The book's order is fit first, then regularize.

code.title: A very large MNIST model (3×2,048 units)
code.original_code:
model = keras.Sequential(
    [
        layers.Dense(2048, activation="relu"),
        layers.Dense(2048, activation="relu"),
        layers.Dense(2048, activation="relu"),
        layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"),
    ]
)
model.compile(
    optimizer="rmsprop",
    loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy",
    metrics=["accuracy"],
)
history_very_large_model = model.fit(
    train_images,
    train_labels,
    epochs=20,
    batch_size=32,
    validation_split=0.2,
)
code.what_it_does: Builds a 784 → 2048 → 2048 → 2048 → 10 MLP, compiles it like the previous models, and trains it with batch size 32. The printed callout on batch_size=32 reads: 'When training larger models, you can reduce the batch size to limit memory consumption.'

line_explanations.explanation: Three hidden Dense layers of 2,048 ReLU units each, then a softmax output over 10 classes.
Same compile configuration as Listing 5.9 and the 2×128 model.
20 epochs, 20% validation split, but batch_size=32 instead of 128. Per the callout, this limits memory use for the larger model.

code.inputs_outputs: Inputs: flattened MNIST images and integer labels. Output: history_very_large_model, whose val_loss is plotted in Figure 5.16.
code.algorithm: Mini-batch RMSprop on crossentropy. With batch 32 there are 1,500 updates per epoch (48,000 / 32), against 375 at batch 128.
code.theory_link: This demonstrates excessive capacity: immediate overfitting.

parameters.name: Dense(2048) ×3
parameters.role: About 10 million parameters in total, which gives huge memorization capacity.

parameters.name: batch_size=32
parameters.role: Smaller batches to limit memory. Also more and noisier updates per epoch.

pitfalls: Changing batch size alongside architecture means the comparison with p.181 is not perfectly controlled. Four times as many updates per epoch also speeds up fitting.
On CPU this model trains much more slowly than the earlier two.

deeper.title: Why the large model is still 'normal' in deep learning
deeper.body: Beyond the book: modern deep learning routinely trains models with far more parameters than samples, and they generalize well thanks to architecture priors, data augmentation, regularization and early stopping. The book's point is not that 10M parameters is forbidden. Without other countermeasures, this much plain-MLP capacity on 48k images overfits immediately, and the best-epoch model (about 0.12) is worse than the 2×128 model's best (about 0.09).

misconceptions.claim: Since it should always be possible to overfit, the biggest model you can afford is always best.
misconceptions.correction: Too much memorization capacity makes the model overfit right away. Its best validation loss (about 0.12) is worse than the medium model's (about 0.09).

misconceptions.claim: Overparameterized models are inherently a mistake.
misconceptions.correction: The book says they are standard. The problem is only the specific symptom of immediate overfitting.

misconceptions.claim: Reducing batch size was done to improve accuracy.
misconceptions.correction: The callout says it limits memory consumption when training larger models.

earlier.note: Figure 5.15: appropriate capacity, and the rule that overfitting is always possible.
Section 5.3's premise: first get a model that can overfit.
Larger batches give less noisy gradients; here the batch is reduced for memory.

takeaways: Too large a model shows itself by overfitting right away.
Overparameterization is standard. Immediate overfitting is the warning sign.
3×2,048 units comes to about 10M parameters. Its best validation loss is about 0.12 at epoch 1, and it climbs to about 0.20.
Reduce batch size to limit memory when models grow.
Once the model can generalize somewhat and can overfit, switch to maximizing generalization (section 5.4).

questions.question: How can you tell, per the book, that your model is too large?
options: Its validation loss plateaus around a fixed value
questions.explanation: That is the stated symptom. A training loss that never decreases is an optimization problem (p.178). A plateau means too little capacity (p.180). Epoch count is not a diagnostic.

questions.question: Why does the very-large-model code use batch_size=32 instead of 128?
questions.answer: To limit memory consumption when training a larger model (the printed callout).
questions.explanation: Activation memory grows with batch size times layer width.

questions.question: How many parameters does the 784 → 2048 → 2048 → 2048 → 10 model have?
questions.explanation: Each Dense layer has inputs×units weights plus units biases.

questions.question: With validation_split=0.2 and batch_size=32, how many gradient updates happen per epoch? Compare with batch_size=128.
questions.explanation: That is four times as many updates per epoch, one reason fitting (and overfitting) happens sooner.

questions.question: When does the book say to switch focus to maximizing generalization?
questions.answer: Once the model has shown some generalization power and is able to overfit.
questions.explanation: That is the opening sentence of section 5.4, consistent with p.177's plan.

questions.question: Comparing Figures 5.15 and 5.16, which model would you deploy if you could stop each at its best epoch, and why?
questions.answer: The 2×128 model. Its best validation loss (about 0.09) is lower than the 3×2,048 model's best (about 0.12, at epoch 1).
questions.explanation: More capacity is not better here: the huge model never goes through a useful learning phase before it starts memorizing.

questions.question: Can you describe the validation-curve signature of each of the three capacity regimes without looking?
questions.answer: Too little: drops and plateaus. Appropriate: dips then rises. Too much: rises from the start.
